panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 9 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I). A: Low-power H&E of the patient's skin biopsy showing a dense dermal histiocytic infiltrate; caption and in-text attribute this to JXG histiocytosis. B: High-power H&E showing numerous multinucleated (Touton-type) giant cells and foamy histiocytes in the dermis, the classic histologic picture of JXG described in the caption and in-text. C: CD68 immunostain with strong cytoplasmic positivity in dermal histiocytes, confirming the non-Langerhans histiocytic phenotype of JXG. D: CD163 immunostain positive in dermal histiocytes, supporting the CD68+/CD1a- non-Langerhans histiocytic phenotype diagnostic of JXG. E: S-100 immunostain negative in the histiocytic infiltrate, excluding Langerhans cell histiocytosis and supporting JXG. F: CD1a immunostain negative, a key discriminator from Langerhans cell histiocytosis and part of the classic JXG immunoprofile. G: Langerin immunostain negative in the dermal infiltrate, further...

in_text_mentions: A 10-month-old male infant was evaluated in the emergency department for multiple papular skin lesions. The lesions had first appeared at six months of age, gradually increasing in number. Upon examination, six well-defined papules with a yellow-orange hue were observed: three on the anterior trunk, one millimetric lesion on the right temporal region, one on the upper back, and one on the eyelid (Figures 1-2). No associated erythema, ulceration, or tenderness was noted. The lesions were firm but mobile upon palpation.

in_text_mentions: A skin biopsy of the lesion was performed. Histopathological examination revealed a dense dermal infiltrate composed of foam cells and multinucleated giant cells of the Touton type, without cytonuclear atypia (Figure 3A). Immunohistochemical analysis (Figure 3B) revealed strong expression of CD68 and CD163 by the histiocytic cells, which were, however, negative for CD1a, CD34, and S100 protein. These findings confirmed the diagnosis of XGJ.

in_text_mentions: Microscopic sections revealed a pandermal infiltrate within the dermis composed of epithelioid and foamy histiocytes admixed with Touton-type giant cells, lymphocytes, eosinophils, and plasma cells. The overlying epidermis shows hyperkeratosis, areas of epidermal thinning alternating with areas of acanthosis with mild elongation of rete ridges. No evidence of atypia, necrosis, or malignancy was identified. Histiocytic cells were positive for CD68. Findings are consistent with JXG (Figures 2-4).

The infant was born by cesarean section, and no complication associated with his birth was documented.

panels.rationale: Single dermoscopic image of a human-patient xanthomatous lesion from an article specifically on dermoscopic patterns in juvenile xanthogranuloma. The caption explicitly describes a xanthomatous lesion with haloed pigment in a peripheral pattern, and the image shows the classic yellow-orange JXG papule. Prior caption triage confirms a real patient dermoscopy with no third-party restriction. The yellow-orange nodule is tagged from the vocabulary; the peripheral pigment network/haloed pigmentation is not in the vocabulary and is proposed. No ethnicity or age is stated for this figure, and no body site is specified.

panels.rationale: Single clinical photograph of a newborn's left flank showing the first erythematous lesion of juvenile xanthogranuloma, as confirmed by the article title, caption, and in-text description. The lesion is an early erythematous papule (red-brown stage) rather than the classic yellow-orange nodule, making it a variant presentation. Histology and IHC in the article confirm JXG diagnosis.

in_text_mentions: On the subject’s third day of life, an erythematous lesion with about 10 mm in diameter appeared on the left flank (Figure 1). Subsequently, similar lesions appear on the abdomen, back, hands, and chin. At the 30th day of life, there were two nodular, firm, yellowish lesions with no inflammatory signs or ulceration, with 10 mm in diameter (Figure 2).

A cutaneous biopsy of the lesion located on the left flank was performed (Figure 1), whose histology revealed presence of histiocytes in the dermis, with no evidence of epidermotropism. The immunohistochemical study demonstrated positivity for cluster of differentiation (CD) 68 and negativity for CD1a, S100, HMB45 and ACL. These results confirmed the clinical diagnosis of NLH, namely JXG.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (H&E, pan-TRK, CD163, Langerin). H&E: H&E histology of the patient's thoracic subcutaneous juvenile xanthogranuloma infiltrate; caption and article identify it as JXG. pan-TRK: Immunohistochemical staining of the same JXG infiltrate showing pan-TRK positivity; article title and caption support JXG attribution. CD163: CD163 immunohistochemical staining of the thoracic subcutaneous JXG infiltrate; supports macrophage/histiocyte lineage in JXG. Langerin: Langerin immunostain of the same JXG infiltrate is negative, supporting the non-Langerhans histiocytic immunophenotype of juvenile xanthogranuloma.

Immunohistochemical staining showed positive reactivity for CD14, CD33, CD45, CD68R, CD163, and factor XIIIa (Fig. 1). The S100 reactivity was inconclusive, with positive staining observed in only a few areas. The following markers were negative: CD1a, CD10, CD30, CD34, CD123, ALK, alpha-actin, BRAF V600E, desmin, EMA, Langerin, myeloperoxidase, and tryptase. Pan-TRK A, B, and C staining was positive, and subsequent RNA gene panel sequencing revealed a TPM3 (exon 7)::NTRK1 (exon 10) fusion transcript. The diag

Five cases, including the index case, showed a positive immunohistochemical reaction on TMA. Notably, the pan-TRK-positive tumors included only xanthogranulomas (4 juvenile and 1 adult xanthogranuloma) and not other non-LCH cases (thirteen Rosai-Dorfman and one Erdheim-Chester disease). Pan-TRK immunohistochemical staining showed a relatively consistent pattern in all 5 positive cases, with diffuse reactivity observed in the cytoplasm. However, there was a notable focal increase in staining intensity along the cell membrane (Fig. 1).

panels.rationale: Single-panel H&E histopathology image from a real patient lesion. Caption and in-text describe dense monomorphic foamy histiocytic infiltration with scattered eosinophils and absent Touton giant cells, with supporting IHC (CD68/factor XIIIa positive, S100/CD1a/langerin negative) establishing juvenile xanthogranuloma in a case presenting as a cutaneous horn (hyperkeratotic lesion). The foamy dermal histiocytic infiltrate is the classic histologic manifestation of JXG and is directly visible; Touton cells are explicitly absent so that finding is not tagged. No third-party copyright indicated; prior triage route is keep. [raw subtype: cutaneous horn]

in_text_mentions: The lesion was excised and a punch biopsy was attained from its base. The hyperkeratotic part, and also the lesion base, was sent for accomplishing histopathologic examination. Although pathologic analysis indicated dense monomorphic foamy histiocytic infiltration, and also scattered eosinophils, there were no Touton giant cells (Figure 2). Since the immunohistochemical staining was positive for CD68/factor XIIa and negative for S100/CD1a/langerin (CD207), the juvenile xanthogranuloma diagnosis was established for the patient.
